en: The Philippine national flower, Sampaguita, is a species of jasmine that releases its sweet fragrance primarily at night to attract pollinating moths.
The Philippine national tree, Narra, belongs to the legume family and has root nodules that host bacteria to fix nitrogen in the soil.
Dr. Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator that uses radiant heat from a hot water bottle to keep premature babies warm without electricity.
The Ifugao people built the Banaue Rice Terraces using an ancient irrigation science that channels rainwater from mountain forests down through the stepped paddies.
The Philippine carabao, the national animal, is a domesticated swamp buffalo scientifically named Bubalus bubalis carabanesis, adapted to thrive in muddy, tropical wetlands.
Filipino physicist Gregorio Zara discovered the physical law of electrical kinetic resistance and invented the two-way radiotelephone, the precursor to modern cellular phones.
The Philippine eagle, the national bird, possesses highly developed binocular vision that allows it to accurately judge distances while diving to catch prey.
The mango, the national fruit, contains high levels of vitamin C and beta-carotene, which are essential nutrients that strengthen the human immune system.
The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a tectonic boundary where moving earth plates cause frequent volcanic eruptions and earthquakes across the archipelago.
Abaca, a Philippine native banana plant, yields the longest and strongest natural plant fibers in the world, making it ideal for weaving durable ropes.
Arnis, the Philippine national sport, requires practitioners to apply biomechanics and physics to generate fast, precise strikes using lightweight rattan sticks.
The Philippines is part of the Coral Triangle, the global center of marine biodiversity, hosting more species of hard corals and reef fish than anywhere else.
